new_statements.quote: Stress is not marked by either Radcliffe-Brown or Man. In none of the languages of the Great Andamanese family (including PGA) is it phonemically relevant. Non-phonemic stress, in all the languages, falls on the initial syllable of the root, at least ordinarily. || Portman 1898: 29: "A line is placed under a syllable to show the stress on it. When a word is not so marked the stress should be placed on the first syllable." || Temple 1903: 115: "Peculiarities of Speech.—Stress in Andamanese is placed on every long vowel, or on the first syllable of the root or stem."
new_statements.citation: Zamponi, Raoul and Bernard Comrie. 2021. A Grammar of Akajeru: Fragments of a Traditional North Andamanese Dialect. London: UCL Press. doi:10.14324/111.9781800080935
new_statements.locator: Chapter 2 Phonology, sec. 2.2 'Stress', p. 22 (PDF page 35). Corroborating primary-era statements: Portman 1898 p.29; Temple 1903 p.115 (both held by the project, page images verified).
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: All three quoted passages verified on the copies we hold in (1) Zamponi & Comrie 2021 (open-access UCL Press PDF), extracted text of PDF page 35 = printed p.22, sec. 2.2 'Stress': 'Stress is not marked by either Radcliffe-Brown or Man. In none of the languages of the Great Andamanese family (including PGA) is it phonemically relevant. Non-phonemic stress, in all the languages, falls on the initial syllable of the root, at least ordinarily.' -- verbatim (only a line-break hyphen in 'phonemi-cally'). (2) Portman 1898 p.29 page image : 'A line is placed under a syllable to show the stress on it. When a word is not so marked the stress should be placed on the first syllable.' -- verbatim; same…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive and by default falls on the first syllable of the root/stem (i.e. root-initial, not on prefixes); Temple adds that long vowels attract stress, and Portman marks per-word departures from initial stress by underlining in his Puchikwar (and other) vocabularies.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: Zamponi & Comrie hedge 'at least ordinarily'; Temple 1903 says stress is also placed 'on every long vowel'; Portman 1898 underlines stressed syllables where stress is not on the first syllable (so non-initial cases exist in his data) and notes (p.390, Aka-Bea) that a root-final long/accented vowel shortens when a suffix or following word is attached.
new_statements.domain_note: Position defined relative to the root or stem (Great Andamanese words carry somatic/possessive prefixes, which by these statements do not take the stress); statements are family-/group-level generalizations from Portman's and Man's 19th-c. transcriptions, not from Apucikwar-specific analysis or recordings (language extinct).
new_statements.identity_note: No Apucikwar-specific stress rule exists in any source opened. The quoted modern statement (Zamponi & Comrie 2021) is in a grammar of Akajeru (akaj1239) and is explicitly scoped to 'all the languages of the Great Andamanese family', which the authors take to include Opuchikwar/A-Pucikwar. The two primary-era statements are likewise group-level: Portman 1898 covers his five 'South Andaman Group' languages, of which 'Puchikwar' is one (his main first-hand Puchikwar documentation, with stress underlined per word in the vocabularies); Temple 1903 says 'Andamanese' and lists 'Bojigyab' (= A-Pucikwar) among the South Andaman languages on the same page.
